name: Bee Gees
hook: Three brothers who began by sounding so like the Beatles that radio played them as the Beatles, then moved to Miami, found a falsetto, and built the biggest disco record of all on a two-bar tape loop.
blurb: The Bee Gees were three brothers, Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb. They were born on the Isle of Man to English parents, grew up partly in Chorlton, Manchester, and started the group in 1958 in Redcliffe, Queensland, Australia. Robert Stigwood managed their international career. Their first big international hit, 'New York Mining Disaster 1941' (April 1967), was sent to American radio in a blank sleeve with a hint that it was by an English group whose name began with B, and DJs played it thinking it was a secret Beatles record. Maurice Gibb later called it a rip-off of the Beatles, and George Harrison told him he had bought it because it sounded like them. In 1975, recording 'Main Course' at Criteria in Miami with the producer Arif Mardin, they moved towards R&B and dance music, and Barry started singing in the high falsetto that defined the rest of their career. Their songs for the film 'Saturday Night Fever' (1977) made the soundtrack the best-selling album in history at the time. When their drummer, Dennis Bryon, had to leave in the middle of recording 'Stayin' Alive' because his mother had died, the group and producer Albhy Galuten tried a drum machine, did not like it, and instead took two bars of drumming from 'Night Fever' and recorded them as a loop on tape, crediting the drummer as 'Bernard Lupe' as a joke. It was a hand-made drum loop on one of the best-selling singles of the decade, years before samplers made that routine. In 1979 a backlash against disco, including Disco Demolition Night and radio stations' 'Bee Gee-free weekends', ended their run in America. Maurice died in 2003 and Robin in 2012.
